extracted.subtask_description: Wartime newswire reporting and field correspondent dispatch procedures — how field reporters and news agencies coordinated, pooled, and were censored during Korean War operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pooling of field dispatches ('pooled story')
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondents in Korea agreed to send only one 'pooled story' of the daily briefing sessions to Tokyo, instead of one in New York; the single story is delivered to the American news agencies in Tokyo for relay abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pooling arrangement was made to offset temporarily tight communications and to avoid duplicate/conflicting reports. It centralizes daily briefings into a single dispatch for international relay (example: "pooled story" of the daily briefing sessions to Tokyo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pooled dispatching to manage limited communications capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the direct link between field headquarters and the Public Information Office in Tokyo was inadequate to carry the heavy, fast flow of news, pooling and a direct teletype circuit were used to manage the load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: pooled messages could be delayed — some messages took six or more hours to reach destinations, the fastest reported was three hours — so pooling trades immediacy for consistency and bandwidth management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field censorship authority over correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Military commanders (example: a colonel and General Walker) were given authority that can include 'full field censorship when or if he deems it necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents operating in the theater can be subject to military-imposed censorship, evacuation or expulsion (example: Marguerite Higgins' expulsion and later reinstatement). Military information control may restrict what reporters can send from the front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military policy on correspondent accreditation and access (including women correspondents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies determine which correspondents may operate at field headquarters — e.g., a previous ban on women correspondents in Korea was lifted by MacArthur, and correspondents could be evacuated or barred until communications/links are adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access and accreditation are controlled by military authorities; changes in policy (lifting or imposing bans) directly affect which reporters may report from the front and under what conditions.
